ety.text: From Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”). Attested in English since 1830. Doublet of mythos.

senses.d: A traditional story which embodies a belief regarding some fact or phenomenon of experience, and in which often the forces of nature and of the soul are personified; a sacred narrative regarding a god, a hero, the origin of the world or of a people, etc.

ex: Myth was the product of man's emotion and imagination, acted upon by his surroundings. (E. Clodd, Myths & Dreams (1885), 7, cited after OED)

senses.d: A commonly-held but false belief, a common misconception; a fictitious or imaginary person or thing; a popular conception about a real person or event which exaggerates or idealizes reality.
ex: Scientists debunk the myth that gum stays in the human stomach for seven years.

senses.d: A person or thing held in excessive or quasi-religious awe or admiration based on popular legend
ex: Father Flanagan was legendary, his institution an American myth. (Tucson (Arizona) Citizen, 20 September 1979, 5A/3, cited after OED)

senses.d: A person or thing existing only in imagination, or whose actual existence is not verifiable.
ex: As for Mrs. Primmins's bones, they had been myths these twenty years.

senses.d: An invented story, theory, or concept.
ex: His story is a pure myth.

ety.text: From Latin mythos m, from Ancient Greek μῦθος m (mûthos).

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”).

First attested as Middle English in 1412. From Middle French mythologie, from Latin mȳthologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “legend”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + λέγω (légō, “to say”). By surface analysis, myth + -ology or mytho- + -logy.

senses.d: The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
A similar body of myths concerning an event, person or institution.
Pervasive elements of a fictional universe that resemble a mythological universe.
ex: This tongue-in-cheek episode is especially fun for people who don’t take their “X-Files” mythology seriously.

senses.d: The set of misconceptions and false attitudes that are held about something and contribute to its perception.
The systematic collection and study of myths.

ety.text: From Late Latin mȳthologia, borrowed from Ancient Greek μῡθολογῐ́ᾱ (mūthologĭ́ā).

Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-der.
